slides.title: Motion Editing
slides.speech: So Go-with-the-Flow makes new videos. But what about the video you already have? Say I've got this clip on top: a bichon and a corgi racing down a sidewalk, and it's basically a tie. The dots and lines are point tracks. The pink one follows the bichon's face through time, the red one follows the corgi's. Now I want the corgi to win. The bottom row is our output. I dragged the corgi's track forward, and the model re-rendered the video so the corgi pulls ahead. Same dogs, same street, same lighting. Only the motion changed. That's MotionV2V: editing the motion of a video that already exists.

slides.title: Why not GWTF?

elements.text: Everything after frame 1 gets made up

slides.speech: So why can't Go-with-the-Flow just do this? GWTF, and pretty much every other motion control method, is image-to-video. It takes the first frame, this one, and generates everything after it. So anything that isn't in frame one, the model makes up. If someone walks in at second three, or the camera turns and shows more of the street, that gets hallucinated, and it's not your video anymore. And the classic editing trick, invert the video and regenerate it, assumes the output lines up with the input frame by frame. A motion edit breaks exactly that.

slides.title: Motion Counterfactuals
slides.speech: So we have to train a model for this, and the problem is data. To learn motion editing you want pairs of videos with the exact same content but different motion, and those don't exist in the wild. Here's how we make them. Start with a real video, this guy walking down the street. Cut a clip out of it. That real clip is the target, the thing the model has to output. Because the target is always real footage, the model always learns to produce real-looking video.

slides.title: Motion Counterfactuals
slides.speech: Then we make a fake version of that same clip with different motion. That's a motion counterfactual. Either we take two frames from the real video and have a video diffusion model fill in between, with a prompt like make him twirl, or we just speed up, slow down or reverse the clip. Then we crop and zoom to fake a camera move. Same guy, same street, different motion. We track points in both, like the dot on his bag. Training is the fake video plus its tracks plus the real tracks in, and the real video out. At test time, your video plays the part of the fake.

slides.title: The Model
slides.speech: Here's test time. Input video: a guy roasting a marshmallow next to a sleeping dog. I click a few points, and a tracker follows them through the video. Those are the source tracks. Then I drag them where I want them to go. Those are the target tracks, in the red box. Yellow means feed the marshmallow to the dog, pink means the dog wakes up. Tracks go in as colored dots on black. The model is a big frozen text-to-video model, CogVideoX, plus a ControlNet-style copy of its first eighteen blocks that reads the input video and both track videos. Same theme as the whole talk: a new handle on a frozen model.

slides.title: Results

elements.text: Picked about 70% of the time over 3 baselines

slides.speech: Left: the ball bounces off the rim, we drag its track down, now it goes through the hoop. Right: retiming, the taxi was ahead and we made the green truck pass it. In a user study, 41 people compared us to ATI, ReVideo and GWTF, and picked ours about 70% of the time for content, motion and overall. On 100 test videos our pixel error is 0.024, versus 0.038 for ATI and 0.067 for GWTF. Limits: past about twenty points it stops following them, and chained edits drift. This is CVPR 2026, with Google. Code isn't out yet. And motion is just one kind of edit. Next, I want any edit.
